questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I chose to study at the University of Tokyo because it was far from Denmark. I wanted something completely new, and it definitely was. I also chose it because of its emphasis on discussion-based teaching, its reputation as the best university in Japan, and one of the best in the world—so I assumed the academic level would be very high. That assumption was somewhat mistaken.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was an incredible experience. I wouldn’t give it a 10/10 because some of the courses I took were purely lecture-based, without practical exercises or much opportunity to process the information in depth.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: The university was great at guiding students through the necessary steps for a smooth transition. There are many small deadlines to keep track of, which can be a bit tedious, but overall, you just need to remember that they want you to succeed and will help you reach your goals. The staff is there to support you, even if it’s easy to forget that sometimes.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer:
There’s an orientation meeting a week before classes start, late september, but it didn’t provide much new information. They showed this website, which I found useful:
https://sites.google.com/g.ecc.u-tokyo.ac.jp/ustep-typeu/accepted-students?authuser=0

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: Just keep track of the deadlines!

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: I got housing in Komaba, which I highly recommend! There’s also a dorm called International Village, but people there are very young and the atmosphere is a bit dull, plus it’s far from the fun parts of the city. Komaba, on the other hand, is right next to Shibuya, making it easy to get around and get home when the night trains stop running. I stayed in Lodge B and paid a little over 2,000 dkk after electricity and water—very basic, but fine. It’s not super social since there aren’t common dining areas, but the residents tend to be slightly older. Komaba Main is another option, where you have your own toilet, but sneaking in guests can be tricky (technically, overnight guests aren’t allowed).

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: There is a simple kitchen with two cooktops. But i never had to wait to make food. You eat your meal in your room which isn't great.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: The lodges are old at depressing but cheap. Main is a nice middle road, they also have dinning rooms.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was fine.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Getting used to the university’s IT system took some effort, but it was manageable. However, their course selection website is quite difficult to navigate.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: Students have one week to try out different courses, but you should attend the ones you plan to take from the very first class. It’s a decent system. If you’re studying in the fall, I recommend scheduling most of your classes early in the week since there are many extended weekends where Mondays are off.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: There’s an office with staff who are very helpful whenever you need assistance. It's called the Global office and is located in the middle of Komaba Campus.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got into all the courses I wanted.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: I’m unsure whether I’d recommend Japanese language courses. They’re structured very much like elementary school classes, and the timing isn’t ideal if you want to finish your main classes early in the week.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I had a lot of questions about the Japanese education system before arriving—and probably even more now. I don’t fully understand how students gain confidence in their knowledge when there are hardly any practical exercises. There are few assignments, and students rarely get to apply what they’ve learned.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I was unsure about which master’s program to pursue, so I took a broad selection of courses pointing in different directions. That wouldn’t have been possible in Copenhagen, at least not with the number of courses I took and the flexibility of just needing to pass as an exchange student. The teaching quality wasn’t particularly strong, but it worked fine for a "gap semester." However, if I were staying for a full year, I think I would have found it frustrating.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
Overall, the academic level was fairly easy, likely because the university accommodates students from very different educational backgrounds and has to find a common denominator, which is the lowest.
There were very few academic resources available when I struggled with something. Often, I had to Google my way through problems, which is difficult for technical topics. At KU, there are many places to seek guidance if you’re unsure about something, which I missed. On the other hand, not having to buy textbooks was nice—but at times, I simply didn’t know where to look for information when I got stuck. That’s not something I’ve experienced at KU.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Neuroscience & Symbols + Mind & Mindfulness → Okay courses.
Sustainable Architecture + History of Architecture in Tokyo → Decent.
Climate Repair → Great professor, lots of discussion.
Material Dynamics 1 & 4 → About large climate systems, a bit boring but informative.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Climate Repair—the professor was fantastic, and the discussions were engaging.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer:
I traveled a lot, which was unexpected but highly recommended!
I walked a lot and campus is right next to the dorm so didn't take to much public transport for chores, only for travelling.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: If you shop at a proper supermarket like OK Everyday Low Price, not My basket or conbini, you can live quite cheaply by cooking at home. Some people claimed eating out is so cheap that cooking isn’t necessary, but I disagree. It’s like eating out in Italy—it might be affordable for a week or two, but over six months, it adds up significantly.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I didn’t join any clubs or circles, though I had planned to. In the end, I didn’t meet anyone who was actively involved in them. Maybe they’re only relevant for long-term students.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: The university occasionally offers discounted tickets for events via email. The student card from UTokyo also provides excellent museum discounts around Tokyo.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Go to Okinawa or Ōshima—amazing island vibes!

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Winters in Tokyo are dry and sunny. It feels like an April/May day in Denmark—slightly chilly, but if you find a sunny bench, you can sit in a t-shirt. That really surprised me. So just use some weekends in Tokyo and go to local markets.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: English is widely spoken in Tokyo. In rural areas, not so much—but with smiles and gestures, you’ll manage. People are generally very kind. So you won't feel to lost and can somewhat adjust fast. It feels very Danish somehow.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: There’s a bit of a højskole atmosphere—many people are eager to meet new friends, so it’s easy to find a group.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Just be respectful and mindful, and you’ll navigate things just fine.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I enjoyed the shrines but the one in Nikko is the greatest. After seeing that you will have seen them all!

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. If you want to specialize deeply in one field, stay in Copenhagen. But if you want to explore a variety of subjects, UTokyo is the place to be. That’s its biggest strength. 
2. Enjoy it, go hiking, and take solo day trips just to wander and explore.
3. Go to Ni-chōme in Shinjuku and party! Many clubs are free and incredibly fun.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: If you live in Komaba, try to take all your classes there. Just avoid Hongo Campus (purely science courses) and International Village.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: It’s a transformative experience—you’ll gain so much confidence and a go-getter mindset.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The only downside? You’ll always want to be outside, experiencing new things—you just can’t relax!

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
